source.title: Uncovering Neural Scaling Laws in Molecular Representation Learning
source.authors: Dingshuo Chen; Yanqiao Zhu; Jieyu Zhang; Yuanqi Du; Zhixun Li; Q. Liu; Shu Wu; Liang Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling behavior in molecular representation learning and reports setup-dependent exponents, as well as settings where performance departs from a power law. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims, rather than reproducing language-model loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study tests molecular task performance against data quantity and model capacity; it does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. Data-pruning comparisons are not recorded as scaling-law rows. Reported curve values are mostly available only in figures, so they are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of molecular-property test metrics (ROC-AUC, AP, MAE) against training-set size. It covers 2D graph, 3D, fingerprint and SMILES encoders, fine-tuning after pre-training, data splits and capacity. These results bear on whether the power-law form holds outside text pretraining (V5) and on setup-dependence and bending of curves (V7). It mostly finds the form holding in a new setting, so T3 fits better than T5. It does not measure language-model loss, compute, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation or shape at fixed parameter count. Its 'downstream' tasks are supervised targets, not downstream of pretraining scale, so V6 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that molecular performance generally follows a power law in data size with no plateau in the range explored. Modality, split, pre-training and capacity change data efficiency; there is no one-size-fits-all configuration. Pre-training lowers the exponent and can cause negative transfer at large downstream sizes. Data-pruning methods do not beat random selection.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised molecular property prediction and molecular representations, measuring ROC-AUC, Average Precision, and MAE against data quantity or capacity. It does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy or scale parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior changes with molecular modality, pre-training, dataset split, model capacity, and the task/model combination. SMILES on MUV and imbalanced MUV at some data scales show departures from the general trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-trained GraphMAE overtakes training from scratch at small downstream sizes but falls behind above about 40K samples on PCBA (negative transfer).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of pre-training shrinks and can turn negative as fine-tuning data grows.

fits_no_version.finding: No clear correlation between dataset size and the capacity needed to reach saturation; a smaller-data task can need a larger model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal model size grows with available data (data-limited analog of compute-optimal sizing).

fits_no_version.finding: Seven data-pruning strategies do not consistently beat random subset selection on PCBA, MUV or HIV (Tables 1, 3, 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data pruning can beat power-law data scaling.

record.problems: The study uses supervised molecular task metrics rather than held-out language-model loss. Most curve values and comparisons are presented in figures without tabulated numerical fit coefficients or uncertainty intervals. It tests only the stated molecular datasets, encoders, and data ranges; PCQM4Mv2 test labels were unavailable, so half the validation set was used as test data.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted for the 60-row limit. The paper also reports fingerprint and SMILES split experiments in Appendix C.3, alternative fingerprint encoders in C.4, different-layer SMILES transformers in C.6, and data-pruning results in Section 3.6 and Appendix C.7; the latter are not rows because they do not directly test a listed scaling-law version.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating small-run fits to much larger runs.
Depth/width at fixed parameter count. Capacity is varied jointly, not at fixed size.
Image/video models, repeated-data training, pretraining loss as the measure. The pretraining data scale itself is not varied.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or pretraining loss.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, alternative fitting methods, and disagreement in compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Fingerprint and SMILES curves under random/scaffold/imbalanced splits. Most follow a power law, but HIV imbalanced/scaffold does not, and SMILES MUV drops again.
MLP vs single-layer Transformer fingerprint encoders; both strongly follow a power law.
SMILES with 1-layer and 3-layer Transformer and RoBERTa; performance drops in the high-data regime on HIV and MUV.
Per-property MUV SMILES curves; most show drops in the last proportions.

Numeric data-scaling values from the random-subset baselines. For example, HIV uniform rises 63.4 to 83.8 from 1% to 80%; MUV imbalanced falls from 72.4 at 60% to 66.3 at 80%. The Table 1 caption says ROC-AUC, though PCBA is reported in AP elsewhere.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is almost entirely figures plus author wording; no fitted exponents or coefficients are tabulated. The text contradicts itself on which split has the largest exponent: the Introduction says random is smallest, Sec. 3.4 says highest. 'Capacity' values are D×W products, not true parameter counts. The metrics are task metrics, not pretraining loss, so V5 support concerns the power-law form only.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power-law fits from smaller runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including how each grows with compute.
Whether depth, width, and other architecture details change loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.

Image and video models, repeated-data training, and language-model training regimes. The tested models are molecular property predictors, and the measured quantities are task metrics rather than pretraining loss.
Language-model downstream task performance and predictability from language-model pretraining loss.
Parameter-counting choices and alternative fitting methods are not compared. Language-model scaling setup and language-model curves are not tested.

relationships.condition: Supervised molecular property prediction (2D GIN, 3D SchNet/PaiNN/SphereNet, fingerprint and SMILES on HIV/PCBA), fine-tuning after GraphMAE pre-training, random/scaffold splits; data range 1%-100% of datasets of about 41K-3.7M molecules
relationships.reason: Log-log metric vs data curves are near-linear with no plateau (r1-r8, r10, r11, r13-r20, r22, r26-r28). The evidence is figures plus author statements, with no fitted coefficients tabulated.
relationships.display_finding: Metric-versus-data curves were nearly linear on log-log axes without a plateau across the tested representations, splits, and fine-tuning settings.

relationships.condition: SMILES Transformer on MUV (and HIV at high data); imbalanced split on MUV
relationships.reason: SMILES on MUV degrades at high data, which the authors say breaks the power law (r12). SMILES drops on HIV per Appendix C.6 (r9). Imbalanced MUV points at 80% and 100% break the fit (r21).
relationships.display_finding: SMILES performance degraded at high data on MUV and HIV, while the imbalanced MUV results at 80% and 100% departed from the power-law fit.

relationships.condition: Scaling in model capacity (GIN, D×W 128 to 6K)
relationships.reason: Larger capacity does not monotonically help: 1.5K is best on HIV and PCBA, and the smallest model (128) is best on MUV (r23-r25).
relationships.display_finding: Performance was nonmonotonic with capacity: 1.5K performed best on HIV and PCBA, while the smallest model, 128, performed best on MUV.

relationships.condition: Molecular data scaling across modality, pre-training, split, capacity and 3D encoder
relationships.reason: Exponents differ by modality, pre-training, split, capacity and 3D model/task, with crossing curves (r8-r11, r13-r20, r22, r23-r28). Curves bend or break for SMILES-MUV, imbalanced MUV and low-capacity PCBA (r12, r21, r25).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents vary with modality, pretraining, split, capacity, and 3D encoder/task, producing crossing curves, while SMILES-MUV, imbalanced MUV, and low-capacity PCBA exhibit bends or breaks.
